title: Resources
text:
This tutorial introduces small area estimation workflows for urban analytics, using direct estimation, area-level Fay-Herriot models, unit-level modelling, and multilevel regression and poststratification using R-INLA.
The tutorial is part of project TRACK-UK by the City Modelling Lab.

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. These indices are used by INLA to attach random effects to the correct area and period.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["msoa_code"]]))
year_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["wave_year"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  msoa_code = area_levels,
  area_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

year_index <- tibble(
  wave_year = year_levels,
  year_id = seq_along(year_levels)
)

To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph .adj as input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point. The boundary file is sorted using area_index so that the graph order matches the area IDs used in the modelling data.


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "msoa_code") |>
  arrange(.data$area_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$msoa_code
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

title: Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
2 Prepare Modelling Data
We then load the area predictors and assemble the modelling data.
The models use two area-level random-effect structures, so we create separate INLA index variables:

area_iid_id indexes the unstructured, independent area effect.
area_spatial_id indexes the structured spatial area effect, which uses the adjacency graph.

Lastly, the sampling variance also needs careful handling before fitting the FH models with INLA. The extent to which the noisy direct estimates will be stablised depends on their sampling variances.

For MSOA-year small areas without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.
Because the outcome is binary (1 for walking daily, 0 otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of 0 when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.


max_variance <- max(
  direct_walk$variance[direct_walk$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

area_covariates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "area_covariates_daily_walking.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "msoa_code",
      "cov_population_density",
      "cov_share_no_car_households",
      "cov_share_work_from_home",
      "cov_share_students",
      "cov_share_routine_semiroutine"
    ))
  )

model_data <- direct_walk |>
  left_join(area_covariates, by = "msoa_code") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "msoa_code") |>
  left_join(year_index, by = "wave_year") |>
  mutate(
    area_iid_id = area_id,
    area_spatial_id = area_id,
    sampling_variance = case_when(
      is.na(.data$direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(.data$variance) ~ max_variance,
      .data$variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ .data$variance
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(.data$wave_year, .data$area_id)

title: Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
3 Fit And Evaluate Models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight.
We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
Baseline
Intercept plus independent area effect


M1
+Temporal
M0 plus temporal random walk


M2
+Core predictors
M1 plus population density and no-car households


M3
+All predictors
M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH)


M4
+Spatial
M3 plus spatial structure among MSOA adjacency




m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$sampling_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
}

model_order <- names(model_formulas)
fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)

Next, we use WAIC as a first check for comparing the fitted model specifications. WAIC, returned by INLA, is a global predictive-fit measure: lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)

4 Compare Stepwise Estimate Changes
At this point the result is just a named list of fitted INLA models. We will collate the fitted values into one results table together with their original direct estimates and sampling variances.


Code
# Main frame to keep from model data
output_cols <- c(
  "msoa_code",
  "wave_year",
  "msoa_name",
  "direct_estimate",
  "variance",
  "n"
)

model_output_frame <- select(model_data, all_of(output_cols))

# Extract fitted values from each model and bind them to the frame
fh_result_tables <- map2(
  fh_fits,
  names(fh_fits),
  function(fit, model_name) {
    fitted_values <- as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)

    model_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values)

    transmute(
      model_results,
      model = model_name,
      across(all_of(output_cols)),
      fh_estimate = .data$mean,
      fh_variance = .data$sd^2,
      has_direct = !is.na(.data$direct_estimate)
    )
  }
)

# Stack model outputs and set display order
fh_results <- bind_rows(fh_result_tables)
fh_results <- mutate(
  fh_results,
  model = factor(.data$model, levels = model_order)
)

4.1 Direct To Baseline Model
We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, spatial structure, or temporal structure to understand how the FH models fundamentally handle noisy direct estimates.


Code
fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per MSOA-year, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    msoa_code,
    wave_year,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m0 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    msoa_code,
    wave_year,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]] - .data$variance
  )

variance_change_limit <- max(abs(direct_to_m0$variance_change), na.rm = TRUE) * .5
direct_variance_limit <- max(direct_to_m0$direct_variance, na.rm = TRUE)

direct_to_m0_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(direct_to_m0, by = "msoa_code")

wave_years <- sort(unique(fh_wide$wave_year))

plot_m0_variance_change <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m0_map_data |>
    filter(.data$wave_year == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$variance_change), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = diverging_low,
      mid = "white",
      high = diverging_high,
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-variance_change_limit, variance_change_limit),
      oob = squish,
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Change"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_direct_variance <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m0_map_data |>
    filter(.data$wave_year == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$direct_variance), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Reds",
      direction = 1,
      limits = c(0, direct_variance_limit),
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Variance"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

5 Adding Predictors
WAIC is useful, but it does not show where estimates change locally or whether those changes are substantive.
For Fay-Herriot SAE models, the final aim is stabilising noisy local estimates. When predictors are added, the model updates the expected value for each MSOA-year. Unstable direct estimates are then pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions, which can improve local accuracy when the predictors are relevant.
For example, moving from M2 to M3 adds the occupation and work-pattern predictors. We map where M3 changes the estimates relative to M2, then summarise the predictor profiles of the areas with the largest upward and downward shifts (top and bottom 10%).

6 Adding Temporal And Spatial Effects
The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be exmined through two diagnostic outputs by INLA:

tau is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. A higher tau means the random effect varies less.
phi is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A value of 0.5 means the structured and unstructured components contribute roughly equally to the area random effect.

The temporal effect has a high tau (6091.734), which means the model estimates only small differences between the three survey waves. The effect is still useful to include because it lets the model account for wave-to-wave changes insteading of treating survey responses from all waves as one.

title: Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
7 Report Final Estimates And Uncertainty
Choosing the final model therefore requires balanced judgement, combining performance diagnostics such as INLA’s WAIC with domain knowledge about the estimand. Where possible, model choice can also be strengthened through further benchmarking, such as comparison with related external indicators or sensitivity checks.
The final model estimates should be reported with their associated uncertainty. For transparency in downstream use of the output datasets, they should also be accompanied by relevant metadata, including the direct estimates, sample sizes, sampling variances, and the modelling specification used to produce them.

  filter(.data$model == "M4 +Spatial")

final_variance_limits <- c(0, max(final_model_results$fh_variance, na.rm = TRUE))
final_wave_years <- sort(unique(final_model_results$wave_year))

    scale_fill_viridis_c(

      na.value = missing_fill,

    theme_void() +

uncertainty_maps <- lapply(final_wave_years, plot_final_variance)

1 The Survey Microdata
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the three survey waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW) in 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are originally geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. Possible to demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.

title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Urban research often needs estimates at fine geographic scales: neighbourhoods, small administrative areas, transport zones, or other local geographies. Survey data are rarely collected at that resolution. Once responses are split by area and time, many cells have small samples, high uncertainty, or no observed respondents at all.
This tutorial introduces spatio-temporal small area estimation (SAE) as a practical workflow for this problem. The aim is to show how survey microdata, direct estimates, auxiliary area data, population information, and spatial-temporal model structure can be combined to produce small area estimates with uncertainty.

title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
1 Why Bayesian inference with INLA?
The tutorial uses Bayesian small area estimation models because they provide a coherent way to combine direct survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, spatial structure, temporal structure, and uncertainty. This is especially useful when some MSOA-year cells have small samples or no observed respondents.
The model-based examples are fitted with INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA is well suited to this workflow because it provides fast Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, including hierarchical, spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal random effects without relying on long MCMC workflows.

title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
2 Tutorial Workflow
The worked example uses the National Survey for Wales to estimate:

Share of adults who walk for transport daily by MSOA-year in Wales over three waves: 2021, 2023, and 2025.







Note



The MSOA-level survey geography used here is synthetically prepared for tutorial purposes. The resulting maps and findings should not be treated as true small area estimates for Wales. More information is provided in the data preparation step.



Prepare data
Build the survey indicator, matched weights, MSOA-year domain, area predictors, unit predictors, and poststratification inputs.
Direct estimation
Produce survey design-based small area estimates and sampling variances. This establishes the baseline and shows where direct estimates are too sparse or noisy.
Fay–Herriot area-level model
Model the direct estimates and their sampling variances using area predictors, temporal effects, and spatial smoothing.
Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model
Model survey microdata directly, then aggregate the fitted relationship to MSOA-year estimates using known area-level predictor means.
Multilevel regression and poststratification
Fit a richer unit-level model and average predictions over population poststratification cells, so the final estimates better reflect the target population structure.

section: 1 Define Domain, Indices And Spatial Graph
text:
1 Define Domain, Indices And Spatial Graph
Before preparing the model inputs, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year in the complete MSOA–year domain. These indices are used by INLA to attach random effects to the correct area and period.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["msoa_code"]]))
year_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["wave_year"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  msoa_code = area_levels,
  area_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

year_index <- tibble(
  wave_year = year_levels,
  year_id = seq_along(year_levels)
)

To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph .adj as input. We again use Queen contiguity.

msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "msoa_code") |>
  arrange(.data$area_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$msoa_code
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

title: Spatio-Temporal Battese-Harter-Fuller Unit-Level Model
text:
3 Fit And Evaluate Models
We fit linear mixed models to respondent-level records, then use them to predict MSOA–year means. This follows the BHF nested-error idea, extended here with temporal and spatial random effects.






Note



The response is binary, so this is a linear probability version of the BHF-style model.


The two models are:








Model
Name
Specifications




M1
Temporal + spatial
Respondent outcome with a temporal random walk and BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+No-car
M1 plus respondent-level no-car access, aggregated using the MSOA Census share of households with no car or van




m1_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  no_car +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 Temporal + Spatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +No-car" = m2_formula
)

INLA does not use a separate predict(newdata = ...) step; instead, it returns fitted values for every row in the input data. We therefore add aggregation MSOA–year rows with indicator = NA for INLA to return fitted values for them.






Note



In the Fay–Herriot model, this feature allows for MSOA–years without survey data (unsampled) to also receive an estimate.



inla_input <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "model",
      indicator,
      no_car,
      year_id,
      area_spatial_id
    ),
  aggregation_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "aggregation",
      indicator = NA_real_,
      no_car,
      year_id,
      area_spatial_id
    )
)

fit_bhf_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = inla_input,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, dic = TRUE)
  )
}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)

WAIC compares the BHF fits to the sampled respondent outcomes. Here, the lower WAIC for M2 shows that adding the no-car predictor improves the temporal-spatial model enough to justify the extra term.

The temporal tau is high, suggesting that the survey-wave adjustments are relatively small. By contrast, the spatial tau is lower, indicating more remaining variation between MSOAs than between survey waves.
Interestingly, the BYM2 phi is high and above 0.5, suggesting that much of the remaining area-level variation in the BHF model is spatially structured. This may look different from the lower phi seen in the Fay–Herriot model, but the two values are not directly comparable. They come from different modelling units and specifications: the BHF model is fitted to individual respondent records, while the Fay–Herriot model is fitted to area-level direct estimates and their sampling variances. The Fay–Herriot model starts from weighted direct estimates and their sampling variances, so it remains closely tied to the design-based survey estimator. The BHF model is fitted directly to respondent records and does not fully account for survey weights or the complex survey design. If some groups are over-sampled, under-sampled, or unevenly distributed across areas, they can pull the fitted unit-level relationship away from the target population.
The model is also under-specified. It only includes no-car access, time, and spatial structure. Adding age, sex, ethnicity, employment status, or other respondent-level predictors would help account for sample composition, but it also raises the data requirement. For aggregation, we would no longer need only the MSOA mean of no_car; we would need a population table giving the joint distribution of all predictors used in the model.
That is the bridge to multilevel regression and poststratification. MRP fits a richer unit-level model, then averages the predicted outcomes over a poststratification table representing the target population. The next workbook takes that step.

The cleaned survey microdata input has one row per respondent-wave for the walking estimand. We use svyby() from the survey package to compute the weighted share and its uncertainty diagnostics for every MSOA-year cell with usable observations. It then completes the MSOA-by-wave grid so missing cells are retained for modelling.

# Define survey design
walk_design <- svydesign(
  ids = as.formula("~1"),
  strata = as.formula("~strata"),
  weights = as.formula("~weight"),
  data = survey_walk
)

# Calculate direct estimate and uncertainty
direct_walk_estimates <- svyby(
  formula = as.formula("~indicator"),
  by = as.formula("~msoa_code + wave_year"),
  design = walk_design,
  FUN = svymean,
  vartype = "se",
  na.rm = TRUE,
  keep.names = FALSE
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    msoa_code,
    wave_year,
    direct_estimate = .data$indicator,
    standard_error = .data$se
  ) |>
  mutate(variance = .data$standard_error^2)

# Calculate sample size per MSOA-year
direct_walk_counts <- survey_walk |>
  group_by(across(all_of(c("msoa_code", "wave_year")))) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Join
direct_walk <- domain_frame |>
  left_join(direct_walk_estimates, by = c(
    "msoa_code", "wave_year"
  )) |>
  left_join(direct_walk_counts, by = c(
    "msoa_code", "wave_year"
  )) |>
  mutate(n = replace_na(.data$n, 0L))

title: Direct Estimation
text:
2 Evaluate Direct Estimates
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because they make three limitations visible:

Uneven temporal and spatial coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and across MSOAs. This means some MSOA-year estimates are based on much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimate over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves. These changes may reflect real behavioural change, but they may also reflect sampling noise.
Zero within-area variance: For binary indicators, especially with small samples, some MSOAs show no within-area variation because all respondents give the same response. This can produce zero or unrealistically low variances.



Code
# Plotting functions
base_map <- function(wave) {
  wave_direct <- direct_walk[direct_walk[["wave_year"]] == wave, ]

  wave_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
    left_join(wave_direct, by = "msoa_code")

  ggplot(wave_data) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_estimate <- function(wave) {
  base_map(wave) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$direct_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "magma",
      limits = c(0, 1),
      labels = share_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Share"
    )
}

plot_uncertainty <- function(wave) {
  base_map(wave) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$variance), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Oranges",
      direction = 1,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      limits = c(0, max(direct_walk$variance, na.rm = TRUE)),
      labels = variance_label,
      name = "Variance"
    )
}

plot_sample <- function(wave) {
  base_map(wave) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$n), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient(
      low = "#fff8e1",
      high = "#4f3b10",
      limits = c(0, max(direct_walk$n, na.rm = TRUE)),
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Sample size"
    )
}


# Generate and assemble plots
e_21 <- plot_estimate("2021") +
  ggtitle("2021") +
  ylab("Direct estimate") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
e_23 <- plot_estimate("2023") +
  ggtitle("2023") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
e_25 <- plot_estimate("2025") + ggtitle("2025")

u_21 <- plot_uncertainty("2021") +
  ylab("Variance") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
u_23 <- plot_uncertainty("2023") + theme(legend.position = "none")
u_25 <- plot_uncertainty("2025")

s_21 <- plot_sample("2021") +
  ylab("Sample size") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
s_23 <- plot_sample("2023") + theme(legend.position = "none")
s_25 <- plot_sample("2025")

diagnostic_panel <- wrap_plots(
  e_21, e_23, e_25,
  u_21, u_23, u_25,
  s_21, s_23, s_25,
  ncol = 3, nrow = 3
) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Share of adults who walk for transport daily",
    subtitle = "Direct estimates, sampling variance, and usable sample size by wave",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )

Model-based approaches are designed to address these issues. Area-level models can stabilise noisy direct estimates by borrowing strength from area-level predictors. Unit-level models go a step further by modelling individual outcomes directly, which helps avoid problems caused by zero or unreliable within-area variance estimates.
